html:
The first printing press in the Americas began work in Mexico City in 1539, less than a century after Gutenberg. Its printer was Juan Pablos, born Giovanni Paoli in Lombardy, who ran the shop as an agent of the Seville printer Juan Cromberger.

The push came from the first bishop of Mexico, Juan de Zumárraga, and the viceroy Antonio de Mendoza, who wanted books for the work of converting the Indigenous peoples. The early books were mostly religious: catechisms, prayer books and guides for priests, several of them in Nahuatl and other Indigenous languages as well as Spanish. Grammars and dictionaries of Indigenous languages followed.

Mexico City had a press for decades before any other city in the Americas. Lima got one in 1584, and English North America not until 1638, near Harvard College. The press helped make Mexico City the intellectual capital of New Spain.
